title: Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan
logline: Sacha Baron Cohen as a Kazakh reporter touring America. Mockumentary with real, unscripted subjects; cringe comedy.
overview: Kazakh journalist Borat Sagdiyev travels to America to make a documentary. As he zigzags across the nation, Borat meets real people in real situations with hysterical consequences. His backwards behavior generates strong reactions around him exposing prejudices and hypocrisies in American culture.

jokes.text: My name Borat. I like you. I like sex. It nice.
jokes.setup: Formal documentary-style introduction of the narrator and his country
jokes.punchline: Immediately derails into 'I like sex. It nice.' — a child-like non-sequitur delivered with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: Perfect character-establishing opener. The blunt pivot from polite introduction to 'I like sex' in broken English is the first definition of Borat's voice — naive, sincere, inappropriate. The economy is excellent: three sentences, complete character established. High character integration because only THIS character delivers this in this way.

jokes.text: It locate between Tajikistan and Kirghistan, and assholes, Uzbekistan.
jokes.setup: Borat narrates Kazakhstan's geographic location in a formal documentary style
jokes.punchline: Uzbekistan is casually dropped in as 'assholes' — an ethnic/national slur delivered as matter-of-fact geographic fact
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure — the rhythm of listing real countries and then the insult lands perfectly. The deadpan delivery makes the absurd nationalism feel like genuine geography. Strong economy and character voice.

jokes.text: This Orkin, the town rapist. Naughty, naughty!
jokes.setup: Borat introduces his town residents as if giving a friendly village tour
jokes.punchline: 'The town rapist' is introduced like a civic role, followed by a playful scolding — as if rape is a minor faux pas
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest jokes in the reel. The structure is perfect: 'town mechanic,' 'town rapist' — the grammatical parallelism makes rape a profession, then 'Naughty, naughty!' reduces it to a mild mischief. It's dark, economical, and could only exist in Borat's worldview. Justifiably scores 8+ — the casual normalization of atrocity through deadpan grammar is genuine craft.

jokes.text: Here, live Muktar Sahanov, our town mechanic and abortionist.
jokes.setup: Borat continues the village tour introducing tradespeople
jokes.punchline: The mechanic is also the abortionist — dual profession delivered as if equally mundane
jokes.explanation: Funny escalation of the village-tour format. The pairing of mechanic and abortionist implies backwoods improvisation that is both dark and absurd. Slightly less sharp than 'town rapist' because it lacks the extra beat ('Naughty, naughty!') that made that joke perfect.

jokes.text: And here, live Muktar Sahanov, our town mechanic and abortionist.
jokes.setup: Continuing the civic tour in the same warm travelogue register
jokes.punchline: The town mechanic moonlights as the abortionist — presented as a perfectly natural dual profession
jokes.explanation: Running the same gag structure a third time (introduce townsfolk with shocking secondary role) but it still earns its laugh. The mechanic-abortionist pairing is specific and funny — the mechanical implication of treating reproductive procedures as automotive repair is dark and absurd. Slightly diminishing returns from the rapist joke but still strong.

jokes.text: He is my neighbour, Nusultan Tudialkbai. He is pailing my assholes.
jokes.setup: Borat introduces his neighbor in a neighborly context
jokes.punchline: 'Pailing my assholes' — Borat means the neighbor is copying everything he does (keeping up with the Joneses), but the malapropism sounds obscene
jokes.explanation: The broken-English malapropism that sounds like a sexual act is a recurring Borat device. Works here because it sets up the keeping-up-with-neighbors bit that follows. Moderate craft — the wordplay is accidental-sounding rather than precisely constructed.

jokes.text: I get a clock radio, he cannot afford. Great success.
jokes.setup: Borat describes petty one-upmanship with his neighbor over windows and steps
jokes.punchline: 'Great success' — Borat's triumphant catchphrase over winning a clock-radio rivalry with a poor neighbor, delivered as if conquering a nation
jokes.explanation: 'Great success' becomes the film's most iconic catchphrase here in its first deployment. The juxtaposition of monumental triumph language for the pettiest possible victory (a clock radio) is perfect character comedy. High quotability — this phrase entered popular culture.

jokes.text: She is my sister. She is number 4 prostitute in all of Kazakhstan. Nice!
jokes.setup: Borat introduces a woman as his sister
jokes.punchline: She is ranked fourth among the country's prostitutes — presented as a proud achievement, punctuated with 'Nice!'
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'number 4' (not 1, not last — but a respectable middle ranking) is brilliant. It implies a formal ranking system for prostitutes, which is funnier than any extreme. 'Nice!' as the capper is perfectly economical. The pride in the delivery is what makes it — Borat is bragging. High quotability, became a signature line.

jokes.text: This is my mother. She is oldest woman in all of Kusek. She is 43.
jokes.setup: Borat introduces his mother as the oldest woman in the village, implying great age
jokes.punchline: She is 43 — the 'oldest woman' is middle-aged by Western standards, implying catastrophic life expectancy in Kazakhstan
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection/setup-punchline. 'Oldest woman in the village' leads the audience to expect something over 80; '43' inverts it completely. Economical and sharp — the dark implication (everyone dies young) is communicated entirely through the number. Strong structure.

jokes.text: And this, my wife, Oksana. She is a Borat. / What did you say about me, you skinny piece of shit? / Why don't you do something useful and dig your mother a grave?
jokes.setup: Borat introduces his wife warmly as part of his village tour
jokes.punchline: His wife immediately turns on him with vicious insults, telling him to 'dig your mother a grave' — revealing the marriage as combative and domestic warmth as pure illusion
jokes.explanation: Good subversion of the warm domestic introduction. 'Dig your mother a grave' is a genuinely inventive insult. The comedic beat works on the contrast between Borat's cheerful framing and the instantly hostile reality. 'Not now, please' from Borat is a nice understated reaction.

jokes.text: This is a VCR-recorded. This are play-cassettes.
jokes.setup: Borat shows off his living quarters like a proud homeowner
jokes.punchline: He shows off a VCR and cassettes as remarkable possessions, implying profound poverty and technological backwardness
jokes.explanation: Functional world-building comedy. The broken English ('This are') and pride in outdated technology establishes Kazakhstan's poverty efficiently. Not particularly inventive on its own but serves the cumulative portrait.

jokes.text: My bed. [visual: a sad, possibly hay-stuffed mattress on the floor or a bench-like sleeping surface]
jokes.setup: Borat gives us a proud interior tour of his home
jokes.punchline: The 'bed' is clearly a primitive, comically inadequate sleeping surface presented with the same pride as any other possession
jokes.explanation: A visual gag relying on the gap between Borat's pride and the actual squalor. Works as world-building comedy and reinforces the character's obliviousness. Less punchy than the verbal jokes but functional for pacing.

jokes.text: My hobbies: Ping-pong. Sun bathed. Disco dance. And on weekends I travel to capital city and watch a ladies while they make a toilet.
jokes.setup: Borat lists hobbies in a cheerful, innocent way — ping-pong, sun-bathing, disco dancing — normal leisure activities
jokes.punchline: The list concludes with traveling to watch women use the toilet, delivered with the same innocent cadence as the previous hobbies
jokes.explanation: One of the best-structured jokes in the reel. The rule of three (ping-pong, sunbathing, disco) establishes a rhythm of normal activities, then the fourth item — watching women use the toilet, presented in the same register — is a perfect subversion. The structure is textbook misdirection, the specific choice of 'ladies while they make a toilet' is both crude and oddly precise. Earns 8+ because the structural craft is genuine.

jokes.text: The Running of the Jew — a festival where giant grotesque 'Jew' caricatures run through town and children must crush the 'Jew egg'
jokes.setup: Borat introduces a local Kazakh festival, framed like a joyous community event
jokes.punchline: The festival is a vicious antisemitic ritual — giant hooked-nose caricatures, a 'Jew egg' that children must stomp — presented as wholesome small-town fun
jokes.explanation: Genuinely audacious satirical comedy. The Running of the Jew is a parody of both the Running of the Bulls and casual antisemitism — by presenting medieval hatred as festive community tradition, it exposes the absurdity of prejudice. The sportscast-style commentary ('She's laid a Jew egg') is brilliantly structured. This is dangerous, deliberate satire rather than mere shock comedy — the craft of the concept is what earns the high score.

jokes.text: Although Kazakhstan a glorious country, it have a problem too. Economic, social and jew.
jokes.setup: Borat lists the country's problems as if reading from a government report: economic, social...
jokes.punchline: '...and jew' — antisemitism is listed as a category of national problem alongside economics and social issues
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — three words do enormous satirical work. The bureaucratic phrasing ('economic, social and jew') mirrors real government problem-classification language and makes bigotry sound like a policy category. It's the perfect button on the Running of the Jew sequence. The compression is what makes it great: no wasted syllables.

jokes.text: No, not film me! Film him! [Azamat objects to being filmed, gesturing at Borat]
jokes.setup: Borat introduces his producer Azamat as they prepare to leave Kazakhstan
jokes.punchline: Azamat, supposedly behind the camera, panics at being filmed and deflects — immediately establishing him as vain, petty, and hypocritical
jokes.explanation: Quick character-establishment beat. Azamat's self-importance and hypocrisy are set up efficiently. Not a complex joke but functional world-building for the duo dynamic.

jokes.text: Urkin, not too much raping... humans only.
jokes.setup: Borat says goodbye to various townspeople before leaving for America
jokes.punchline: 'Humans only' — the qualifier implies that the default is non-human, making the warning both darker and more absurd
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The callback to 'the town rapist' is tight, but the genius is in 'humans only' — it doesn't just repeat the earlier joke, it escalates it. The implication that animal rape is the default requiring a specific caveat is a brilliant dark absurdist twist. Exceptional economy (three words carry the whole joke), and the callback structure rewards attentive viewers. Comfortably earns 8.5.

jokes.text: Doltan, I'll get you a new arm in America.
jokes.setup: Borat says farewell to townspeople
jokes.punchline: Borat promises to get his friend a new arm in America — implying the man has a missing arm, treated as a minor errand
jokes.explanation: The casualness of promising to pick up a prosthetic arm like a souvenir is funny in its breezy sincerity. Relies on the visual of a one-armed man for full impact. Decent dark-comedy economy.

jokes.text: Wave goodbye to your clock radio, asshole!
jokes.setup: Borat shouts a final farewell from the departing vehicle
jokes.punchline: Callback to the clock radio that his neighbor couldn't afford — Borat's final petty triumph as he leaves
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback that deepens the character. Borat's last act before leaving for America is to taunt his neighbor about a clock radio. The 'asshole' makes it funnier — the pettiness escalating to genuine hostility. Good economy, strong character integration.

jokes.text: If you cheat on me, I will come over there and snap off your cock.
jokes.setup: Borat's wife gives him a farewell message as he departs
jokes.punchline: Instead of a loving goodbye, she threatens gruesome genital mutilation for infidelity
jokes.explanation: Oksana's departure threat is funny primarily because it perfectly mirrors the hostile marriage dynamic established earlier. The specific threat ('snap off your cock') lands as dark comedy because it's so literal. Sets up the later payoff when this exact threat becomes relevant to the plot.

jokes.text: I arrive in America's airport with clothings, US dollars and a jar of gipsy tears to protect me from AIDS.
jokes.setup: Borat narrates his arrival at JFK airport, listing what he brought
jokes.punchline: 'A jar of gipsy tears to protect me from AIDS' — a folk remedy listed alongside money and clothes as a rational travel essential
jokes.explanation: Brilliant absurdist construction. The list structure (clothing, money, then...) sets up a rational expectation, then 'gipsy tears' introduces magical thinking, and 'to protect me from AIDS' gives it a specific medical purpose that makes it funnier than a generic superstition. The logic is internally consistent within Borat's worldview, which is what makes it land rather than just being random. The layering of two prejudices (against Roma and AIDS fear) is characteristically dense.

jokes.text: New Yorkers react with hostility to Borat's attempts to greet them — 'My name mind your own fucking business' / 'Get the fuck out of here before I break your jaw'
jokes.setup: Borat innocently tries to introduce himself to strangers on the street in New York
jokes.punchline: Real New Yorkers respond with escalating aggression, unaware they're being filmed
jokes.explanation: Classic Borat real-world interaction comedy. The gap between his sincere friendliness and the authentic hostility of New Yorkers is funny, and 'My name mind your own fucking business' is a great accidental comedy line from a real person. The escalation from cold dismissal to explicit threats amplifies the joke. The comedy here is partly in the unscripted reactions.

jokes.text: Hotel check-in: 'We'll call it 85.' / 'We'll call it 117. Let me get the door for you.'
jokes.setup: Borat attempts to haggle the hotel room rate from $117 down to $85
jokes.punchline: The clerk completely ignores the haggle and firmly restates the price with cheerful professionalism — the American system is not negotiable
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure ('We'll call it X') is well-constructed and the clerk's calm dismissal mirroring Borat's phrasing is funny. Culture-clash comedy — Borat's bazaar-haggling instincts meeting American fixed-price commerce.

jokes.text: Borat mistakes the elevator for his hotel room and announces 'Pack your things. We'll be moving again shortly.'
jokes.setup: Hotel clerk escorts Borat to his room; they enter an elevator
jokes.punchline: Borat believes the elevator is his room and immediately starts complaining about being downgraded, ordering Azamat to pack up
jokes.explanation: Classic fish-out-of-water visual gag — the elevator-as-room confusion is a well-worn setup but executed well because Borat's complaint ('I will not move to a smaller room') adds character specificity. His indignation is funny.

jokes.text: King in the castle. King in the castle. Have a chair. I have a chair. Go do this, go do this. I king in the castle.
jokes.setup: Borat reaches his hotel room for the first time
jokes.punchline: He erupts into a childlike triumph dance, chanting 'King in the castle' — a pure id explosion of joy at having a hotel room
jokes.explanation: Pure character comedy. The specific chant ('King in the castle') and the childlike repetition capture something genuine about Borat's innocence beneath the offensive surface. Visually funny and quotable. The hotel clerk's silent presence watching this is an implied reaction beat.

jokes.text: Just dry him, no hand relief.
jokes.setup: Borat is being groomed/prepared before an interview — presumably dried off
jokes.punchline: 'No hand relief' — Borat instructs his groomer to dry him without sexual service, implying this is normally offered/expected
jokes.explanation: Very economical dark joke. 'No hand relief' as a grooming instruction implies a service economy where sexual favors accompany basic grooming, delivered as a matter-of-fact modifier. The specificity ('hand relief' rather than a cruder term) makes it funnier.

jokes.text: How is my back pussy? — Not bad. Moist.
jokes.setup: Borat asks his groomer about the condition of an area on his back
jokes.punchline: 'Back pussy' — apparently a real word in his vocabulary for some back feature; 'Not bad. Moist.' is a clinical response that plays entirely straight
jokes.explanation: The clinical exchange ('Not bad. Moist.') elevates what could be just a crude non-sequitur. The deadpan response makes it funnier than if someone reacted in shock — the total normality of the exchange is the joke.

jokes.text: Should I make joke about my mother-in-law? In America, that's a very popular joke.
jokes.setup: Borat meets a humor coach to learn American comedy
jokes.punchline: He immediately reaches for the most clichéd possible joke category — mother-in-law jokes — as his first question
jokes.explanation: Setup for a longer comedic sequence. The irony that Pat Haggerty, a humor coach, earnestly confirms that mother-in-law jokes are indeed popular is a mild self-aware joke about American comedy's lowest-common-denominator.

jokes.text: I have sexy time with my mother-in-law? — A what time? — Sexy time.
jokes.setup: Humor coach asks if Borat has a mother-in-law joke
jokes.punchline: Borat's 'joke' is actually a confession that he had sex with his mother-in-law — said sincerely, not as a joke
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The structure is perfect: 'Mother-in-law joke?' → Borat gives a 'joke' that is actually a sincere account of incest → 'No, it is not a joke.' The punchline within the punchline ('No, it is not a joke') is the master stroke — his insistence that this is real life, not humor, while Pat tries to make sense of it. 'Sexy time' as a Borat coinage also earns its place in the cultural vocabulary here. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Do you ever laugh on people with retardation? / My brother Bilok have a very funny retardation.
jokes.setup: Humor coach explains Americans don't make fun of things people can't choose, like disability
jokes.punchline: Borat immediately volunteers that his brother has 'a very funny retardation' — the specific positive framing ('very funny') is the joke
jokes.explanation: Setup for the cage story that follows. 'Very funny retardation' is a good line because the qualifier ('very funny') implies Borat is treating disability as an entertainment category with varying quality ratings. The coach's patient response adds to the cringe.

jokes.text: Sometime, my sister, she show her vagin to my brother and say 'You will never get this!' He, behind his cage, crazy-crazy, everybody laughing. But one time, he break the cage, and he get this. And then we all laugh. High 5!
jokes.setup: Borat describes a family entertainment involving his disabled brother in a cage
jokes.punchline: The story escalates: (1) disabled brother caged, (2) sister taunts him sexually, (3) he escapes and assaults her, (4) everyone laughs including Borat who offers a high five to the audience
jokes.explanation: One of the most memorable moments in the film. The story is a perfect escalating structure: each revelation is worse than the last, culminating in Borat offering a high-five to Pat Haggerty (a real humor coach reacting to a real scripted monologue) while completely sincere. The 'High 5!' is the masterstroke — it invites the audience to participate in approving something atrocious, and Pat's horrified non-response is implied in the cut. The structure matches the 'Snip snap' anchor: escalating horror + physical punctuation + expectation of shared joy. Earns 8.5+ — this is the standout joke of the reel.

jokes.text: The NOT joke lesson — 'This suit is black NOT' / 'This suit is black pause NOT' / 'This suit is black pause NOT' repeated while Pat Haggerty corrects and Borat cannot understand the pause
jokes.setup: Pat Haggerty tries to teach Borat the 'NOT' joke format
jokes.punchline: Borat literally says the word 'pause' out loud and can't grasp that the pause is implied — the lesson degenerates into absurdist repetition
jokes.explanation: Brilliant sustained comedy bit. 'This suit is black pause NOT' is a perfect joke about language being literal — Borat has no access to implicit meaning, so when told there's a pause, he says 'pause.' The repetition escalates the absurdity and Pat Haggerty's increasing frustration (a real humor coach) is unscripted. The meta-joke about joke structure is clever. The escalating variations ('This suit is black-not,' 'This suit is black pause NOT') are individually funny. This is among the best extended bits in the reel.

jokes.text: Everybody say USA television much better, but this I watch for three hours and do not change. This two arrows to change the channel.
jokes.setup: Borat sits in front of his hotel TV, narrating to camera
jokes.punchline: He has been watching the same channel for three hours because he can't work the remote — 'this two arrows' referring to the channel-change buttons he doesn't understand
jokes.explanation: Fish-out-of-water technology gag. Funny because Borat has referenced his VCR as a prized possession — a TV remote is alien technology. The specificity of 'three hours' and his confusion about the arrows makes it more grounded than a generic 'doesn't understand tech' joke.

jokes.text: This CJ was like no Kazakh woman I have ever seen. She had golden hairs, teeth as white as pearls. And the ass hole of a 7 years old.
jokes.setup: Borat narrates falling in love with 'CJ' — a woman he sees on TV — describing her beauty in romantic terms
jokes.punchline: The list of her beautiful qualities culminates in 'the ass hole of a 7 years old' — a grotesque non-sequitur delivered as the ultimate compliment
jokes.explanation: One of the most perfectly constructed jokes in the reel. The setup follows the classic beautiful-woman description trope (golden hair, white teeth like pearls) — establishing romantic, elevated language — then pivots to the most disgusting possible compliment, delivered with identical sincerity. The specificity of '7 years old' (not just 'young') is what makes it land as a pure joke rather than mere shock. The structure is textbook misdirection. High quotability, iconic. Earns 8.5+.

jokes.text: In Kazakhstan, it is illegal for more than 5 women to be in the same place. Except for in brothel or in grave.
jokes.setup: Borat introduces the concept of feminist groups in America, contrasting with Kazakhstan
jokes.punchline: The only legal exceptions to the women-gathering law are brothels and graves — the two categories of women the patriarchy permits
jokes.explanation: Superb dark satirical construction. The list of two exceptions (brothel, grave) captures the full spectrum of how misogyny either sexualizes or kills women. It's compressed satire — the two nouns do what a paragraph of feminist theory would do. The deadpan delivery as national law makes it funnier. This is the kind of joke that makes you laugh then feel slightly ashamed, which is the intended effect. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: So what does this feminism mean? / It's the theory that women should be equal to men. / [Borat laughs]
jokes.setup: Borat asks the feminist veterans to explain feminism, as if genuinely curious.
jokes.punchline: He laughs at the concept of gender equality as if it's the most absurd thing he's heard — the feminist's exasperated 'You are laughing. Well, that is the problem' is the deadpan counter.
jokes.explanation: A reliable cringe-comedy beat using the feminist veterans as straight-men. The laugh is the punchline — Borat's involuntary reaction to 'women should be equal to men' says everything about his worldview. The feminist's response ('that is the problem') is an unintentionally sharp meta-commentary.

jokes.text: But is it not a problem that a woman have a smaller brain than a man? / That is wrong. / But a government scientist doctor lama prove that it is size of squirrel.
jokes.setup: Borat attends a feminist meeting and asks sincere questions about women's equality
jokes.punchline: He invents an authoritative source ('government scientist doctor lama') to back up his claim that female brains are squirrel-sized, escalating the authority citation with each noun
jokes.explanation: The chain of authority ('government scientist doctor lama') is excellent — it accumulates credential words until 'lama' (Tibetan monk) makes the whole thing collapse. The specificity of 'size of squirrel' (not 'smaller' but measurably squirrel-sized) is funny. The feminist's earnest rebuttal amplifies the cringe.

jokes.text: Give me a smile, baby. Why angry face? / Well, what you say is very demeaning. Do you know the word demeaning? / No.
jokes.setup: A feminist is explaining why Borat's comments are offensive
jokes.punchline: Borat doesn't know the word 'demeaning' — which perfectly illustrates that he has no conceptual access to the category of harm he's causing
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat. 'Give me a smile, baby' to a feminist is funny in its obliviousness. The 'do you know the word demeaning? / No' exchange is a sharp illustration of the film's satirical thesis: prejudice and ignorance are indistinguishable from each other.

jokes.text: I could not concentrate on what this old men were saying. All I could think about was this lovely woman in her red water panties.
jokes.setup: Borat narrates his experience at the feminist meeting
jokes.punchline: He calls the feminists 'old men' and is fixated on a woman's 'red water panties' (swimsuit) — his lust completely overwhelms any interaction with their message
jokes.explanation: 'Red water panties' as a description of a swimsuit is a good Borat coinage — precise but wrong in a way that reveals cultural ignorance. The irony of being unable to focus on a feminist presentation because of sexual fixation is on-point for the character.

jokes.text: She from a town called the Baywatches. / She's just on television. Her name was Pamela. / Do she live here in New York? / She lives in California. / He's gonna look her up.
jokes.setup: Borat mentions the woman he saw on TV ('CJ') and asks if the feminists know her
jokes.punchline: He calls Baywatch 'the town called the Baywatches' — treating a TV show as a real geographic location — and when told she's in California, another feminist mutters 'He's gonna look her up' (anticipating a stalking plotline)
jokes.explanation: 'The town called the Baywatches' is a genuinely funny Borat coinage — the article 'the' and the plural make it sound like he's describing a geographical region. The unscripted feminist's aside ('He's gonna look her up') is a perfect ironic comment that plants the entire second-act premise.

jokes.text: Although I was obsessed by this CJ, I could not pursue her. Or else my wife will snap off my cock.
jokes.setup: Borat narrates his conflicting desires after leaving the feminist meeting
jokes.punchline: His wife's specific earlier threat ('snap off your cock') becomes the actual logical barrier to pursuing his love interest
jokes.explanation: Good callback that integrates the earlier threat into actual plot logic. Funny because Borat accepts the threat completely at face value as a rational deterrent. The specificity of 'snap off my cock' landing in a romantic-longing context is well-timed.

jokes.text: Dear Boratsendiev, your wife Oksana was walking your retarded brother in the woods when a bear attacked and violated and break her. She is now dead.
jokes.setup: Borat receives a telegram, which he asks the deliverer to read
jokes.punchline: The telegram reports his wife's death by bear attack — but includes the specific detail that the bear 'violated and break her' before killing her, delivered in telegram-formality register
jokes.explanation: The telegram's formal register colliding with the content ('violated and break her') is well-constructed. The specific sequence — bear attack, violation, breaking — is both horrifying and absurd. Sets up the punchline of Joke 43 perfectly.

jokes.text: Pearl Harbor is there... and so is Texas.
jokes.setup: Borat argues with Azamat that they should travel to California; Azamat asks what's there
jokes.punchline: Borat lists Pearl Harbor (which is in Hawaii) and Texas (which is not in California) as reasons to go to California
jokes.explanation: Perfect character-comedy geography joke. Borat's confident, specific citation of things that aren't in California ('Pearl Harbor is there') is funny because his American geography knowledge consists entirely of famous names with no spatial awareness. The addition of Texas doubles the joke.

jokes.text: He insist we do not fly, in case the Jews repeated their attack of 9/11.
jokes.setup: Borat explains why they're driving rather than flying across America
jokes.punchline: Azamat believes Jews perpetrated 9/11 and might repeat it — a matter-of-fact conspiracy theory delivered as a reasonable travel precaution
jokes.explanation: Dark satirical joke about antisemitic conspiracy theories. The framing as a practical safety concern ('in case the Jews repeated their attack') is what makes it comedy rather than offense — by treating the conspiracy theory as the kind of reasonable precaution a traveler takes, it exposes its absurdity. Ties into the film's ongoing antisemitism-as-satire thread.

jokes.text: But then it look like I'm holding a gipsy while I eat my hram.
jokes.setup: Driving instructor tells Borat to use two hands on the steering wheel
jokes.punchline: Borat objects because two-handed driving looks like holding a Roma person while eating pork — an inexplicable cultural association delivered with utter sincerity
jokes.explanation: Genuinely bizarre and funny. The specificity of the objection — the visual comparison is so strange that it creates genuine absurdist comedy. 'Hram' (Borat's pronunciation of 'ham') adds an additional layer. The driving instructor's real-world reaction to this explanation is implied.

jokes.text: Must not hit the children. / Look, there is a woman in a car. Can we follow her? And maybe make a sexy time with her?
jokes.setup: Instructor warns Borat to watch the children while driving
jokes.punchline: Borat dutifully repeats the instruction ('Must not hit the children') then immediately asks to stalk and sexually assault the woman in the next car
jokes.explanation: Perfect tonal whiplash. The 'Must not hit the children' dutifully repeated shows Borat trying to be a responsible driver, then the immediate pivot to asking to follow and assault a woman shows his moral compass is entirely inverted. The structure — compliance then escalation — is well-crafted.

jokes.text: Because a woman has a right to choose who she has sex with. — What!? They do? — There must be consent. — How about that. That's good, ha? — It's not good for me.
jokes.setup: Driving instructor explains that a woman must consent to sex
jokes.punchline: Borat is genuinely surprised and interested that women have this right, asks 'That's good, ha?' — seeking validation — and the instructor says 'It's not good for me'
jokes.explanation: One of the best scenes in the reel. The unscripted driving instructor's honest response ('It's not good for me') is comedy gold — a real American adult admitting that women's sexual autonomy is inconvenient for him. This is the film's satirical thesis in miniature: by drawing out unfiltered responses from real people, Borat reveals authentic attitudes that polite society suppresses. The 'What!? They do?' from Borat is perfect wide-eyed discovery. This earns 8+ because the construction is elegant and the real-world revelation is exactly what the film is designed to do.

jokes.text: Hey, don't look at me. Eat my teets. / That will eat your shit. / You fuck my mother.
jokes.setup: Borat shouts at a car that is following them, apparently road-raging back
jokes.punchline: Borat's road-rage insults are surreal malapropisms — 'Eat my teets,' 'That will eat your shit,' 'You fuck my mother' — an escalating sequence of broken-English aggression
jokes.explanation: Funny primarily for the malapropism sequence. 'Eat my teets' as a road-rage insult is a genuinely inventive broken-English construction. The escalation to 'You fuck my mother' is a good button. The instructor's mounting panic adds to the scene.

jokes.text: I like you? Do you like me? / I do like you. / You are my friend? / You're a nice young man and I am your friend. / Will you be my boyfriend? / I won't be your boyfriend. / Why not? You don't like me? / Don't push, I can be.
jokes.setup: In the aftermath of the road-rage incident, Borat needs reassurance from the instructor
jokes.punchline: 'Don't push, I can be' — the instructor softens on being Borat's 'boyfriend' after initially refusing, suggesting Borat has worn him down with earnest neediness
jokes.explanation: Another brilliant unscripted exchange. The escalation from 'I like you' → 'friend' → 'boyfriend' and the instructor's reluctant 'Don't push, I can be' is a perfect slow-crumble of a real person being gradually maneuvered into an uncomfortable position by Borat's sincerity. The driving instructor's 'Don't push' implies he's genuinely considering it, which is the joke.

jokes.text: Will you be my boyfriend? / I won't be your boyfriend. / Why not? You don't like me? / Don't push, I can be.
jokes.setup: Borat has asked the driving instructor if they are friends
jokes.punchline: He escalates from friendship to 'will you be my boyfriend?' — and Mike's negotiated 'Don't push, I can be' suggests he's actually on the fence
jokes.explanation: Mike's 'Don't push, I can be' is the real laugh — he's essentially saying yes under pressure to a driving student's request to be boyfriends. His obvious discomfort but eventual capitulation to social pressure is a perfect real-subject moment. The scene mines genuine awkwardness from a real person's response.

jokes.text: I want to have a car that attract woman with a shave down below. — That would be a Corvette. Or a Hummer.
jokes.setup: Borat asks a car salesman for a car that attracts women with a specific description
jokes.punchline: The salesman confidently recommends Corvette or Hummer based on Borat's description — which was a crude sexual reference — without registering the double meaning
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the car dealership sequence. The salesman's smooth, professional response to a request involving sexual grooming descriptions is funny — he processes 'attract woman with shave down below' as market research data.

jokes.text: A man, yesterday, tell me, if I buy a car, I must buy one with a pussy magnet. — He means a car that women would like. — Yes, but where you keep this magnet? — No, no there's no magnet... women love the Hummers. — Do this have a pussy magnet? — No. — If I give you good price, will you please put in pussy magnet? — There's no such thing in this country as a magnet.
jokes.setup: Borat has heard the phrase 'pussy magnet' and interprets it as literal automotive equipment
jokes.punchline: He repeatedly demands a physical magnet be installed in the car, escalating to offering to pay extra for one — the salesman's increasingly exasperated explanation that it doesn't exist is the running joke
jokes.explanation: Good sustained bit. Borat taking 'pussy magnet' literally and asking to have one installed is a great idiom-literalism joke. The escalation ('If I give you good price') and the salesman's confused but professional response ('There's no such thing in this country as a magnet') is an unscripted real-world response that is funnier than anything scripted could be.

jokes.text: If this car drive into a group of gipsies, will there be any damage to the car? — It depends on how hard you hit them. — Hard! — If somebody rolls on the windshield, it could crack your windshield. — How fast do I need to go to guarantee I kill them? — With this vehicle right here, probably doing 35-40 mph will do it.
jokes.setup: Borat asks a practical question about the vehicle's durability against Roma people
jokes.punchline: The salesman engages seriously with the question of how fast you need to drive to kill Roma people, providing a specific speed estimate ('35-40 mph') — an unscripted real answer to a question about murder
jokes.explanation: One of the most audacious pieces of comedy in the reel. The horror is that the car salesman engages with the question entirely professionally — calculating windshield damage and kill-speed for hitting Roma people as if answering a crashworthiness question. The specificity of '35-40 mph' is what makes it devastating: a real American professional provided a real answer to a question about murder. This is Baron Cohen's satirical method at its sharpest — the target of the joke is not Borat but the man who answered him. Earns 8.5+ — the originality and real-world impact are exceptional.

jokes.text: When I buy my wife, at the start, she was cook good, her vagin work well, and she strong on plow. But after three years, when she was 15, she become weak... and her vagin hang like sleeve of wizard.
jokes.setup: Borat compares buying a wife to buying a car — a warranty analogy
jokes.punchline: The list of his wife's qualities at purchase ('vagin work well,' 'strong on plow') is bad enough; 'when she was 15' (meaning she was 12 when purchased) escalates to dark territory; 'vagin hang like sleeve of wizard' is the absurdist image that lands the whole sequence
jokes.explanation: The single most quotable line in this reel and one of the most famous in the film. 'Sleeve of wizard' as a metaphor is a stroke of comedic genius — it's simultaneously absurdist, specifically visual, and utterly unlike anything in the comedic vocabulary. The structure is perfect escalation: (1) functional wife specs, (2) the horror of 'when she was 15' (meaning child bride), (3) physical deterioration described as aging machinery, (4) the wizard-sleeve punchline. The car-warranty framing is what makes it work as a sustained bit. This is the strongest single line of the reel and arguably the film. Earns 8.7 — close to the best-ever anchor.

jokes.text: I am looking for something between 600-650 dollars. — We don't have cars for 650. — I might be able to sell you a ho-sale car, for 700, with no warranty.
jokes.setup: After inspecting a $52,000 Hummer, the salesman asks Borat's budget
jokes.punchline: Borat's budget is $650 for a vehicle. The salesman tries to work with it and offers a 'wholesale' car — Borat has negotiated himself from a $52k Hummer to a junker with no warranty
jokes.explanation: Good button on the car dealership sequence. The specificity of '$600-650' (not even a round number) for a vehicle, delivered after inspecting a $52,000 Hummer, is a good punchline. The salesman's professional pivot to find something in that range is an authentic response that makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Chevrolet guarantees that with the warranty.
jokes.setup: Borat has just described the terrifying physical deterioration of his wife, asking if the car will do the same
jokes.punchline: The salesman responds that the Chevrolet warranty covers this — straight-facedly applying a standard sales pitch to the most un-warrantable situation imaginable
jokes.explanation: The salesman's straight pivot to the warranty pitch after the 'sleeve of wizard' speech is genuinely hilarious because it suggests he has processed the whole thing as a standard consumer concern and has the boilerplate answer ready. His professionalism in the face of the insane is the joke. Perfect straight-man economy — one sentence is all it needs.

jokes.text: Borat spots the Kazakhstan embassy and shouts 'Fuck you, mother fuckers!' at it
jokes.setup: Borat narrates arriving in Washington D.C. to learn from American politics, framing himself as a respectful foreign journalist
jokes.punchline: He immediately screams profanity at his own country's embassy, revealing a deep personal grudge that is never explained
jokes.explanation: The joke works on pure surprise and character revelation. Borat's earnest diplomatic framing is instantly shattered by the outburst, and the fact that it's directed at his own country's embassy adds absurdist specificity. It's economical and perfectly in character — Borat is simultaneously a proud Kazakh nationalist and deeply ambivalent about his homeland.

jokes.text: Borat offers Bob Barr cheese, explaining 'My wife, she make this cheese... She make it from a milk from her tit.'
jokes.setup: Borat presents cheese as a diplomatic gift to a real former U.S. Congressman, framing it as a cultural custom
jokes.punchline: The cheese is revealed to be made from his wife's breast milk — Barr has already accepted and presumably handled it
jokes.explanation: The joke's structure is near-perfect: the revelation comes AFTER Barr has already accepted the cheese, maximizing cringe retroactively. Barr's polite 'Very nice' before the punchline makes the audience complicit in his discomfort. The delay between acceptance and revelation is a masterclass in comedic timing. The phrase 'from a milk from her tit' has just enough broken-English charm to be both crude and oddly poetic.

jokes.text: Bob Barr's visible discomfort reaction upon hearing the cheese is breast-milk — his face and attempt to maintain composure
jokes.setup: Barr has already accepted and praised the cheese
jokes.punchline: He must now process that he was just handed homemade human breast-milk cheese and maintain diplomatic composure
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat extends joke #2 and is inseparable from it. Barr's real, unscripted response to learning what he just touched/accepted is half the joke. The fact that he's a real politician makes his struggle to stay polite both funny and uncomfortable.

jokes.text: Borat narrates over Gay Pride Parade footage: 'People here were much more friendly than in New York'
jokes.setup: Borat stumbles into a Gay Pride Parade after his political interview
jokes.punchline: His innocent, positive observation — 'much more friendly than in New York' — lands as profound dramatic irony given what he is about to describe happened to him there
jokes.explanation: Works as a setup for the Alan Keyes revelation. Borat's obliviousness is total — he genuinely enjoyed the parade and made friends, unaware of the community he was in. The understatement is funny precisely because the audience sees what's coming.

jokes.text: Borat describes his Gay Pride Parade encounter to Alan Keyes: 'I invite them back to my hotel room, we drink like a normal in Kazakhstan, we wrestle like a normal in Kazakhstan, then they say I wash you in the shower, he wash me in the shower.'
jokes.setup: Borat presents an apparently wholesome account of making friends at a Sunday parade in Washington
jokes.punchline: Each additional detail ('wrestle,' 'wash you in the shower') escalates the obvious sexual nature of the encounter that Borat is completely oblivious to, recounting it to a staunchly conservative politician
jokes.explanation: This is one of the reel's best constructions. The triple escalation (drink → wrestle → shower washing) mimics the classic rule-of-three, with each step being more explicit than the last while Borat's narration grows more domestic and innocent ('like a normal in Kazakhstan'). The target audience for this confession is Alan Keyes — a 2-time Republican presidential candidate with vocally anti-gay positions — which makes the cringe near-unbearable in the best way. The character integration is exceptional: only Borat, with his genuine cultural obliviousness, could deliver this.

jokes.text: 'You telling me that man who tried to put rubber fist in my anus was homosexual?'
jokes.setup: Alan Keyes has just explained what 'gay' means after Borat's shower story
jokes.punchline: Borat's dawning comprehension introduces an entirely new, more extreme detail that was not part of his earlier account — the rubber fist — suggesting the encounter went considerably further than described
jokes.explanation: This is the reel's standout joke. The structure is a masterwork: Borat has already told the full story (drink, wrestle, shower), and the audience thinks the escalation is complete. The reveal of the rubber fist as an afterthought — framed as a question about sexual orientation, not as the shocking detail it is — is a perfect comedic bomb. The delivery ('was homosexual?' with genuine bewilderment) and Alan Keyes's visible struggle to respond compound the impact. The economy is extraordinary: seven words ('tried to put rubber fist in my anus') carry an enormous payload. The joke is both wildly quotable and deeply character-specific: Borat's total innocence about what happened to him is the engine. This is comparable in structural excellence to the vasectomy anchor example.

jokes.text: Borat narrates: 'Even though my anus was broken, I knew that rest of our journey would be great success.'
jokes.setup: Following the rubber fist revelation
jokes.punchline: Borat treats severe anal injury as a minor inconvenience and pivots immediately to optimism about the road trip
jokes.explanation: The deadpan understatement here is superb. 'My anus was broken' is a stunning euphemism used with complete earnestness, and the pivot to optimism ('I knew that rest of our journey would be great success') is perfectly incongruous. The sentence treats a grotesque trauma as equivalent to, say, a flat tire. High quotability — 'my anus was broken' has genuine catchphrase potential.

jokes.text: Borat is introduced on a live local TV news broadcast as 'Borhat Sahadyev' — his name mangled
jokes.setup: A local TV anchor warmly introduces their special international guest by name
jokes.punchline: She gets his name completely wrong ('Borhat Sahadyev'), establishing the anchor's lack of preparation for this segment
jokes.explanation: Minor joke that sets up the TV segment. Functional but not memorable — the name mangling is a small observational detail about media incompetence rather than a crafted comedic moment.

jokes.text: Borat attempts to ask the anchor to signal when they start, while they are already live on air: 'can you tell me because I want to make your ends and then I come back here and... if you tell me what me on the we start... / We started. We are actually live on the air right now.'
jokes.setup: Borat claimed he is a 'TV professional' moments earlier
jokes.punchline: He is completely unprepared and incoherent while already broadcasting live — directly contradicting his self-described expertise
jokes.explanation: A solid callback that pays off the 'TV professional' claim immediately. The anchor's flat correction ('We are actually live on the air right now') is a good straight-man beat. The irony of a self-proclaimed professional being this chaotic on live TV is well-executed.

jokes.text: Borat excitedly waves and shouts 'Hello, US and A!' repeatedly to the camera on live television
jokes.setup: He is told they are live; a normal guest would collect themselves
jokes.punchline: Borat erupts into childlike excitement, repeatedly shouting the same greeting at the camera with increasing enthusiasm, derailing the segment
jokes.explanation: Borat's childlike enthusiasm is consistent with his character. 'Hello, US and A!' is a running character motif. The repetition escalates slightly but doesn't have a true punchline — the joke is entirely in the performance.

jokes.text: 'When you come to Kazakstan, you can stay my house, you can sleep my house and you can use my sister.'
jokes.setup: Borat is on live TV, apparently extending warm hospitality to the anchor in a cultural exchange
jokes.punchline: The hospitality escalates from 'stay' to 'sleep' (already slightly odd) to 'use my sister' — treating a woman as a usable commodity, delivered with total sincerity on live TV
jokes.explanation: Brilliant three-beat structure: stay/sleep/use. The first two are normal hospitality; the third is a grotesque non-sequitur that reframes Borat's culture as casually transactional about women. The live TV setting amplifies the horror. The anchor's response is a cut to the weather, suggesting the show panicked. Economy is near-perfect — 'use my sister' is three words that carry enormous payload.

jokes.text: Immediately after 'use my sister,' the anchor hard-cuts to meteorologist Ted Johnson for the weather
jokes.setup: Borat has just offered his sister to the anchor on live television
jokes.punchline: The show immediately pivots to weather with zero acknowledgment, as if the safest move is to pretend it didn't happen
jokes.explanation: The abrupt cut is itself the punchline — a classic 'we're moving on' panic response from real local TV people dealing with an unscripted disaster. The juxtaposition of 'use my sister' with 'Meteorologist Ted Johnson with the latest on tropical storm...' is genuinely funny structural editing.

jokes.text: Borat wanders onto the weather set mid-broadcast and asks 'Very nice have me. What your name?' to the meteorologist
jokes.setup: The station has fled to the weather segment to escape Borat; the meteorologist is doing a live weather report
jokes.punchline: Borat physically intrudes on the weather segment and treats the meteorologist like a new friend he's just met at a party
jokes.explanation: The physical intrusion onto the weather set escalates the TV segment's chaos nicely. The meteorologist's attempt to continue the weather while Borat socializes is a good sustained cringe beat.

jokes.text: 'He is a she? — Somehow!'
jokes.setup: Borat is redirected away from the meteorologist toward someone named Adrianne
jokes.punchline: He is surprised Adrianne is a woman (suggesting he expected a man from the name), and the staff member's response 'Somehow!' is an oddly loaded confirmation
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny exchange. The 'Somehow!' from the staff member carries an unexpected edge, possibly ad-libbed, which gives it a slight spark of authenticity.

jokes.text: A rodeo official advises Borat to shave his moustache so he doesn't 'look like a terrorist' and suggests he could pass as Italian
jokes.setup: An official is giving Borat pre-rodeo advice
jokes.punchline: The advice is casual, matter-of-fact racial profiling — shave the moustache so you don't look Muslim, pass as Italian — delivered without any self-awareness by a real American citizen
jokes.explanation: The joke's power is that it's entirely real — a genuine American official casually advising ethnic camouflage. The comedy is dark and uncomfortable, with the film using Borat's presence to expose real attitudes. The 'pass as Italian' detail is particularly absurd and specific.

jokes.text: The rodeo official talks about hanging terrorists from the gallows and about jailing/hanging gay people, with Borat enthusiastically agreeing
jokes.setup: Borat has asked about gay people; the official is sharing his views
jokes.punchline: The official advocates hanging gay people, which Borat enthusiastically agrees with ('In my country, they take them... to jail and finish them') — the comedy is the horrifying alignment of a real American official with a fake Kazakh reporter on executions
jokes.explanation: One of the film's key satirical moves: the fictional Borat and the real American official find common ground on executions, exposing genuine bigotry. The comedy is uncomfortable and dark rather than laugh-out-loud, but it's effective and purposeful satire.

jokes.text: The man refuses Borat's customary kiss greeting — 'The people that do the kissing over here are the ones that float around like that' (gesturing to imply gay men)
jokes.setup: Borat attempts to kiss the man on the cheeks as a greeting, consistent with European/Central Asian custom
jokes.punchline: The man refuses, associating male cheek-kissing exclusively with homosexuality, unaware of the irony given Borat's recent Gay Pride Parade experiences
jokes.explanation: A mild joke that works as social satire — the man's homophobia around something as innocuous as a greeting. The irony that Borat recently had a rubber fist in his anus adds a layer for the audience. Not one of the film's stronger moments but consistent with the scene's satirical thrust.

jokes.text: Borat at the rodeo: 'We support your war of terror'
jokes.setup: Borat is addressing a large patriotic crowd at a rodeo, expressing support for the U.S.
jokes.punchline: 'War on Terror' becomes 'war of terror' — a malapropism that accidentally reverses the meaning, though the crowd initially cheers
jokes.explanation: A deceptively brilliant single word swap. 'War OF terror' instead of 'war ON terror' inverts the entire meaning — the U.S. is now the terrorists — and the crowd cheers before processing it. The economy is perfect: one preposition change carries the entire satirical payload. The character integration is strong: Borat's ESL-style errors make the malapropism plausible while still pointed.

jokes.text: 'May George Bush drink the blood of every single man, woman and child of Irak.'
jokes.setup: Borat has been offering increasingly patriotic-sounding toasts to the crowd about killing terrorists
jokes.punchline: The escalation reaches vampiric imagery — George Bush drinking blood — which is so extreme it becomes absurdist, delivered with the same earnest patriotic cadence as the lines before it
jokes.explanation: The escalation across the rodeo speech is excellently structured: 'support your war of terror' → 'kill every single terrorist' → 'drink the blood of every man, woman and child.' Each line is cheered by the crowd until the vampiric imagery crosses a line the crowd can't follow. The speech is a satirical masterpiece about how jingoistic rhetoric can be escalated to literal monstrousness without anyone noticing until it's too late. The blood-drinking line is the peak and is genuinely quotable.

jokes.text: 'May you destroy that country so that for the next thousand years not even a single lizard will survive in their desert.'
jokes.setup: Following the blood-drinking toast, Borat continues escalating
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'not even a single lizard' — a cold-blooded animal that barely registers in human concern — as the benchmark for total annihilation is both absurdly funny and chilling
jokes.explanation: The lizard detail is what elevates this from generic dark humor to genuinely original writing. 'Not a single lizard' as the ultimate measure of desolation is both poetic and absurd — it's almost biblical in scale while being anchored to this tiny, ridiculous specific creature. The 'thousand years' adds to the mock-epic grandiosity. This is Borat's satirical writing at its most precise.

jokes.text: Borat sings 'Kazakhstan National Anthem' to the tune of The Star-Spangled Banner — 'Kazakhstan is the greatest country in the world / All other countries are run by little girls'
jokes.setup: Borat announces he will sing the Kazakh national anthem to the tune of the American national anthem; the crowd is patriotically primed
jokes.punchline: The lyrics are a surreal celebration of Kazakhstan's potassium exports and casual homophobia ('All other countries is the home of the gays'), delivered to the anthem melody while the crowd slowly realizes this is not what they expected
jokes.explanation: The Kazakhstan national anthem sequence is one of the film's most celebrated set pieces. The genius is structural: by using the melody of The Star-Spangled Banner, Borat tricks the audience into a reverent posture, then fills that form with absurd content (potassium exports, 'run by little girls'). The escalation from mildly weird to outright offensive ('home of the gays') mirrors the crowd's dawning horror. The specificity of potassium as the national pride detail is inspired — specific enough to seem real, absurd enough to be funny. The gap between form (sacred national anthem) and content (potassium supremacy) is the entire joke.

jokes.text: Borat spots a house and declares it a 'Gypsy village,' intending to 'extract some of their tears' to remove a curse
jokes.setup: Borat and Azamat are demoralized and looking for a sign
jokes.punchline: He identifies a normal American farmhouse as a Gypsy village and his solution to their misfortune involves harvesting Gypsy tears as a magical cure
jokes.explanation: The 'Gypsy tears' bit is a good absurdist construction. Borat's folk superstitions are presented as genuine problem-solving logic, which is funny precisely because of how earnestly he pursues it. The specificity ('extract some of their tears') is well-chosen.

jokes.text: Borat approaches the homeowner: 'Do not fear me, gipsy. All I want from you is your tears. Let's give them to me or I would take them.'
jokes.setup: Borat believes the house is a Gypsy village and needs tears for a curse removal
jokes.punchline: His opening gambit is to simultaneously try to be non-threatening ('do not fear me') while immediately threatening to forcibly take her tears ('or I would take them'), delivered completely straight
jokes.explanation: The self-contradiction of 'do not fear me / or I would take them' is a small gem. The logic is: reassure, explain benign need, then immediately threaten. It's perfectly in character (Borat has no self-awareness that this is threatening) and economical. The homeowner's baffled response is unscripted and genuine, adding to the cringe.

jokes.text: Borat points to a child's doll: 'Who is this lady you shrunk? Was she the owner of this house that you came in front of?'
jokes.setup: Borat is inspecting the homeowner's possessions, believing she is a Gypsy witch
jokes.punchline: He genuinely believes the doll is a shrunken real person — consistent with his superstitions — and constructs an elaborate accusation around it
jokes.explanation: The 'shrunken person' interpretation is a great absurdist detail. Borat's accusation is internally consistent with his worldview (Gypsies shrink people) and is delivered with the gravity of a genuine criminal investigation. The homeowner's dazed response is unscripted and real.

jokes.text: Borat and the homeowner both see a Baywatch VHS tape and simultaneously say 'Baywatch' with the same reverence
jokes.setup: Borat has been treating the house as full of sinister magical objects
jokes.punchline: Both Borat and the homeowner — who are in a state of mutual suspicion — instantly bond over shared Baywatch reverence, breaking the tension completely
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical moment. The word 'Baywatch' spoken by both simultaneously, with identical reverence, says everything — it's a cultural touchstone that transcends Borat's foreign status and the homeowner's wariness. It also sets up the eventual Pamela Anderson quest. Two words, perfectly timed, maximum laugh.

jokes.text: Young Black men tell Borat he looks like Michael Jackson and should 'Beat It'
jokes.setup: Borat has stopped to ask for directions in what appears to be a Black neighborhood
jokes.punchline: The men immediately clock Borat's appearance and compare him to Michael Jackson — the reference is both an insult and an oddly specific cultural comparison that only works because of Borat's vaguely processed look
jokes.explanation: A mild improvised moment from real people. Funny in context but not craft-driven comedy — it's a reaction from genuine subjects rather than a constructed joke.

jokes.text: Borat asks the young men to teach him how to dress and act 'like them,' and earnestly takes style and language lessons
jokes.setup: Borat has just been told he looks like Michael Jackson; he pivots immediately to asking these strangers for cultural assimilation lessons
jokes.punchline: He genuinely tries to learn — including 'loosen up your belt,' showing his underwear — with complete earnestness, with the men playing along as impromptu etiquette teachers
jokes.explanation: The earnest cultural exchange is funny and somewhat sweet. Borat's total willingness to transform himself (he immediately starts showing his underwear) is in character and the men's genuine enjoyment of teaching him adds warmth.

jokes.text: One of the men teaches Borat a phrase: 'You gotta lick it, before you kick it.'
jokes.setup: The men are teaching Borat street vernacular
jokes.punchline: The phrase is sexual slang taught as general vocabulary to a foreigner who will presumably deploy it in completely inappropriate contexts
jokes.explanation: Decent setup for future misuse, though the payoff happens off-screen. The implied comedy of Borat using this phrase in polite company is funnier than the moment itself.

jokes.text: Borat attempts to use his new street vocabulary at what appears to be a fraternity/suburban home: 'What's up with it, vanilla face? Me and my homie Azamat just park our slab outside, we're looking for somewhere to post up our black asses for the night. So, bang-bang, skid, skid, nigger.'
jokes.setup: Borat has just received a crash course in street slang and is immediately applying it to find lodging
jokes.punchline: He deploys the vocabulary with no contextual understanding — 'vanilla face,' 'post up our black asses,' and finally the slur — to a presumably white suburban household, creating an instant social catastrophe
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff of the language lesson sequence and it's well-executed as a callback. The escalating misuse of learned slang — culminating in a slur delivered in the wrong context to the wrong people — is a portrait of how language without context creates disaster. 'Bang-bang, skid, skid, nigger' as the conclusion suggests Borat is filling gaps in his memory with approximations. The homeowner's flat 'Leave now or we'll call the cops' is a perfect straight-man response. The structure is strong because we've seen where the vocabulary came from, making the deployment funnier.

jokes.text: Borat narrates: 'We can't stay here, they are player haters.'
jokes.setup: They have just been threatened with the police for Borat's racist vocabulary deployment
jokes.punchline: Borat's takeaway from being threatened with arrest is simply that the residents are 'player haters' — the hip-hop vocabulary applied with complete sincerity to explain systemic rejection
jokes.explanation: Three words, enormous payoff. Borat has absorbed the vocabulary but not the meta-awareness — 'player haters' as an explanation for racism-induced police threats is both funny and oddly insightful as an accidental parody. The economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Borat and Azamat whisper in bed: 'They're Jews. — I know that now. Look if we can stay here. We cannot stay here, they are motherfuckers. They'll kill us. We need to escape.'
jokes.setup: An entirely kind and welcoming Jewish couple has given them a room
jokes.punchline: In hushed, terrified tones, Borat and Azamat treat their lovely hosts as mortal threats — the extreme disconnect between the evident reality and their paranoid fantasy is the joke
jokes.explanation: The gap between the real situation (a lovely couple offering dinner and a room) and Borat's paranoid terror is extremely well-executed. The whispered 'they are motherfuckers / they'll kill us' while presumably feet away from people bringing sandwiches is genuinely funny. The scene is satirizing antisemitism by showing how deranged it is — these are demonstrably kind people.

jokes.text: Borat narrates in bed at 3 AM: 'It is three in the morning, I am in the nest with jews. They have cleverly shifted their shapes. One of them has taken the form of a little old woman.'
jokes.setup: Borat and Azamat are terrified of their Jewish hosts; the hosts are clearly normal elderly people
jokes.punchline: Borat has convinced himself that the Jews have used shapeshifting magic to disguise themselves as elderly people — the specific detail of 'a little old woman' as a terrifying disguise is perfectly absurd
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best comedy constructions. The shapeshifting Jews conspiracy theory is a real antisemitic trope, and Borat deploys it with terrified sincerity — but the specific 'shape' they've chosen is 'a little old woman,' which is both the least threatening possible form and deeply funny as a 'clever disguise.' The narration style (documentary voiceover delivered from under covers at 3 AM) compounds the absurdity. 'You can barely see her haunts' is a surreal bonus line.

jokes.text: Borat and Azamat's panicked escape from the B&B at 3 AM — throwing money at the cockroaches they believe the hosts have transformed into
jokes.setup: Borat has narrated that the Jews have further shifted their shapes; we see what appears to be coins/bills being thrown at cockroaches or some small creatures on the floor
jokes.punchline: Their solution to the 'shape-shifted Jews' is apparently to bribe them with money — playing into the antisemitic trope that Jews are motivated by money, used by Borat with total sincerity as a tactical solution
jokes.explanation: This is satirically brilliant. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) the absurdism of throwing money at cockroaches, (2) the antisemitic trope of bribing Jews with money used as a sincere tactical solution, (3) the panic of two grown men terrified of an elderly couple's home. It's dark humor that exposes how internally consistent bigotry is as a worldview — Borat uses Jewish stereotypes to solve his Jewish-stereotype problem.

jokes.text: Borat says: 'Let's go back to New York, at least there's no Jews there.'
jokes.setup: Borat and Azamat are fleeing the B&B
jokes.punchline: New York — one of the cities with the largest Jewish population in the world — is presented as a Jew-free safe haven
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — one line, enormous comedic payload. The irony of choosing New York as a Jew-free destination is so perfectly wrong that it functions as an inadvertent exposure of Borat's total ignorance. The line is highly quotable and captures the film's satirical approach to antisemitism in nine words.

jokes.text: Borat asks a gun shop clerk: 'What is the best gun to defend from a Jew?'
jokes.setup: Borat and Azamat need 'protection' for their journey; they enter a gun shop
jokes.punchline: His stated purpose for needing a gun — defending against Jews — is not met with the outrage one would expect; the film lingers on the clerk's response
jokes.explanation: The joke has two targets: Borat's antisemitism AND the gun shop clerk's response (a 9mm or .45 is recommended — a matter-of-fact professional recommendation without any apparent pause to question the target). The clerk's response ('I would recommend either a 9mm or a 45') is devastating satire of gun culture's neutrality about stated intent. Economy is near-perfect: six words carry enormous satirical weight.

jokes.text: Gun shop clerk's response to 'best gun to defend from a Jew': 'I would recommend either a 9mm or a 45.'
jokes.setup: Borat has asked for gun recommendations for killing a Jew
jokes.punchline: The clerk responds as if this is a completely normal inquiry with professional product recommendations, with no apparent shock or objection
jokes.explanation: The clerk's calm, professional response is the second half of a two-part satirical joke. His apparent non-reaction to 'defend from a Jew' — going straight to caliber recommendations — is simultaneously the film's funniest and most disturbing moment. As a standalone deadpan response, the economy is extraordinary. The joke would not exist without Borat's setup but the clerk's reaction is what makes it land.

jokes.text: Borat at the gun shop: 'I, movie star, Dirty Harold. Come on and make my name, jew.'
jokes.setup: Having been recommended guns, Borat is now apparently performing his version of Dirty Harry
jokes.punchline: 'Dirty Harold' instead of 'Dirty Harry' and 'make my name, jew' instead of 'make my day, punk' — both mangled simultaneously, with the slur replacing the original insult
jokes.explanation: Double mangling of the quote: wrong name (Harold/Harry) AND wrong target word (jew/punk). The misquotation reveals Borat has absorbed American pop culture imperfectly — he knows the pose and vibe of Dirty Harry but substitutes his own cultural preoccupations into the punchline. Very character-specific.

jokes.text: Borat asks a pet shop: 'What type of dog is this?' The clerk answers: 'This is a tortoise.'
jokes.setup: Unable to buy a gun (not a citizen), Borat seeks animal protection
jokes.punchline: He asks what kind of dog a tortoise is — either genuinely unable to identify it or committed to the idea that any animal could be a dog
jokes.explanation: Simple but effective absurdist beat. The clerk's straight answer ('This is a tortoise') is a perfect deadpan straight-man delivery. The brief exchange is efficiently funny.

jokes.text: Borat: 'Is this a cat in a hat?' Clerk: 'No, it's a tortoise in a shell.'
jokes.setup: Borat has just been told the animal is a tortoise
jokes.punchline: He attempts a Dr. Seuss reference, misapplying it to a tortoise; the clerk's straight correction ('No, it's a tortoise in a shell') inadvertently echoes the same rhyme structure
jokes.explanation: The accidental rhyme in the clerk's correction ('tortoise in a shell' mirrors 'cat in a hat') adds a bonus layer. Borat's attempt to use a cultural reference he's absorbed imperfectly is on-brand, and the clerk's response has unexpected poetry.

jokes.text: Borat mishears 'retired' as 'retarded': 'You are retard? — Yes. Physical or mental? — Retired. — Not retarded.'
jokes.setup: Borat is making polite dinner party conversation and asking about occupations
jokes.punchline: He hears 'retired' as 'retarded' and immediately follows up with the clinically diagnostic 'physical or mental?' — a question that would be offensive in any context but is delivered here with complete concern and earnestness
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best constructed jokes. The misunderstanding is plausible (retired/retarded do sound similar), and the follow-up question 'Physical or mental?' shows Borat taking the information seriously and trying to categorize it properly — which is both logical within his frame and devastating in its implication. The three-way exchange (yes/physical or mental?/retired/not retarded) is perfectly structured with great economy.

jokes.text: Borat asks the dinner guests: 'Do you have a telephone in this village?'
jokes.setup: Borat is making polite dinner conversation at a Southern American home
jokes.punchline: He calls the community a 'village' — suggesting he perceives American towns as equivalent to rural Kazakh settlements — and questions whether they have basic infrastructure
jokes.explanation: Economic and character-specific. 'Village' as a descriptor for an American suburb and the genuine inquiry about telephone access neatly inverts expected cultural hierarchies. Good economy.

jokes.text: Borat shows a photo of his son: 'He very strong. — My goodness, is that him lifting you?' followed by 'He grow 6 centimetre and now is 17 centimetre long.'
jokes.setup: Borat is sharing family photos at the dinner table, apparently a culturally appropriate thing to do
jokes.punchline: The photo appears to show his son lifting him (strength); the follow-up dimensions ('17 centimetre long') clearly refer to penis size — the guests are looking at what is apparently a photo of his son's genitals
jokes.explanation: The reveal is well-structured: physical strength is established first (is he lifting you?), then the dimensions are given in a way that only makes sense if the measurement is not of the son's height. The hostess's 'I'm not sure one would show this photo to...' is a perfectly restrained reaction. The proud-father framing makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Borat pays compliments: 'You have a very gentle face and a very erotic physique.' — to a Southern etiquette coach
jokes.setup: He has been instructed to pay compliments to people at the dinner table, 'only if you truly agree'
jokes.punchline: His sincere compliment combines 'gentle face' (acceptable) with 'very erotic physique' (deeply inappropriate in any dinner party context), delivered as if these are equivalent observations
jokes.explanation: The two-part structure (gentle face / erotic physique) is well-calibrated: the first part is reassuring and lowers defenses, the second subverts it completely. The fact that Borat was explicitly instructed to 'only compliment if you truly agree' makes this worse — this is his genuine assessment, carefully considered.

jokes.text: Guest: 'That's a very good observation.' — to 'very erotic physique'
jokes.setup: Borat has just called the etiquette coach's physique 'erotic' at a formal dinner
jokes.punchline: A guest at the table responds with 'That's a very good observation' — either sincerely agreeing or responding on autopilot in a politeness reflex
jokes.explanation: The genuine guest response is the punchline to joke #48. Whether sincere or reflexive, 'That's a very good observation' applied to 'erotic physique' at a formal dinner is a perfect deadpan reaction beat. The film captures real social lubrication at work — people defaulting to positive responses even when blindsided.

jokes.text: Borat points at the etiquette coach and asks her husband 'She is your wife?' then looks at the host: 'In my country, they would go crazy. For this two, not so much...'
jokes.setup: He has just called the etiquette coach's physique erotic; now he's identifying relationships at the table
jokes.punchline: He enthusiastically endorses the coach's attractiveness ('they would go crazy') while dismissively rating the actual wife and her companion as unattractive ('not so much') — to their faces
jokes.explanation: The pivot from complimenting the wrong woman to dismissing the actual wife is well-structured. 'Not so much...' delivered with casual finality to someone's face is excellent cringe comedy. The trailing ellipsis in the delivery implies there's more bad news he's decided not to share.

jokes.text: Borat asks the etiquette coach: 'What should I say if I need to go to the shit-hole?'
jokes.setup: The etiquette lesson continues; Borat is apparently absorbing the lessons and now has a practical question
jokes.punchline: 'Shit-hole' as the word requiring a polite substitute — the extended negotiation over the right term ('restroom' / 'bathroom' / 'toilet' / 'brown...') while Borat helpfully mimes makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: The extended negotiation over bathroom vocabulary is a good sustained cringe sequence. Borat's attempts at approximation ('the brown... bad, bad thing from...') are funnier than the initial question.

jokes.text: Borat returns from the bathroom carrying a bag of his own feces and asks the hostess where to put it: 'Thank you very much, I feel much better. Cindy, where should I put this?'
jokes.setup: Borat has excused himself to the bathroom after the elaborate shit-hole vocabulary lesson
jokes.punchline: He returns carrying what is visually established to be a bag of excrement, treating its disposal as a natural social inquiry for his hostess
jokes.explanation: This is one of the reel's high-impact moments. The elaborate setup (vocabulary lesson, excusing himself properly) makes the return with actual feces a perfect payoff. The casualness of 'I feel much better / where should I put this?' treats human excrement as a normal hostess-delegated logistical problem. The formal dinner party setting maximizes the cringe. It's genuinely shocking but earned by the buildup.

jokes.text: The etiquette coach then attempts to explain how to use toilet paper; Borat asks if the host cleans the guest's anus: 'The host cleans the anus of the other? — No, no, no. Nobody touches you except you.'
jokes.setup: The coach is now trying to explain post-toilet hygiene (after the bag incident)
jokes.punchline: Borat has apparently experienced host-assisted wiping in Kazakhstan, and must be informed that in America, anal hygiene is a solo activity
jokes.explanation: Extends the bathroom sequence with another absurdist Kazakh cultural assumption. The coach's patient 'Nobody touches you except you' implies this had to be explicitly stated, which suggests Borat's experience of bathroom assistance in Kazakhstan is taken as given.

jokes.text: Borat asks if he may bring a guest to dinner; the coach says yes if you ask in advance; Borat then immediately produces Luenell — a sex worker — at the door
jokes.setup: He asked about bringing a guest theoretically; the etiquette coach gave standard protocol advice
jokes.punchline: The 'guest' is immediately revealed — she was apparently waiting outside — and Borat introduces her as his friend Luenell, then shortly after as a prostitute, to this Southern etiquette dinner party
jokes.explanation: The misdirection is excellent: the question about guests seemed academic, so the immediate arrival of a guest (who was evidently already there) subverts expectations. The structure — polite theoretical question, polite answer, immediate reality — is well-constructed. The reveal of Luenell as a prostitute to a Southern etiquette dinner party is the ultimate payoff.

jokes.text: Borat is thrown out of the dinner party; as the hostess is calling the police, Borat asks: 'Why you call police? Has the retard escaped?'
jokes.setup: The dinner has collapsed; the hostess is calling the sheriff; Borat is being ejected
jokes.punchline: Borat's mind goes immediately to his earlier 'retarded' guest (actually the retired man), suggesting he thought there was a genuinely disabled guest at risk of wandering off
jokes.explanation: Superb callback. Borat never processed the retired/retarded correction, so his mental model of the dinner party still includes a 'retarded' guest he's concerned about. 'Has the retard escaped?' in a moment of crisis is brilliant — it's simultaneously the worst possible thing to say AND reveals Borat's genuine concern for this person he thinks has a disability. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Borat introduces Luenell to people at a bar: 'Hi, my name Borat. This my friend, Luenell. She is a prostitute.'
jokes.setup: They have left the dinner party; Borat is introducing Luenell in a bar setting
jokes.punchline: He introduces her occupation ('prostitute') as casually and proudly as one would introduce a doctor or teacher — no shame, no whisper, full public announcement
jokes.explanation: The casualness of announcing someone's sex work as a social introduction detail is well-executed. Borat's total lack of social calibration about which information is typically shared in introductions is the character joke. The rhythm of 'my name Borat / this my friend Luenell / she is a prostitute' has an almost haiku-like structure.

jokes.text: Borat declines to go home with a woman after a rodeo (Luenell?): 'I would like very much... but I in love with a woman in Malibu.
