It would be nice to her for me to... / If you ever in town again, look me up.' — 'If I ever in town again, Luenell, I would very much like to pay you for sex.'
jokes.setup: Luenell has asked Borat in for the night; he declines out of loyalty to Pamela Anderson
jokes.punchline: His chivalrous refusal is followed by a promise to 'pay you for sex' the next time he's in town — combining romantic loyalty to Pamela with a commercial transaction offer to Luenell, treating both relationships as equally normal
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Borat is being genuinely sweet and gallant (refusing out of love for Pamela), and the offer to pay for sex next time is delivered as an equivalent act of consideration — like saying 'I'll take you to dinner next time.' He's not being crass; he thinks this is a thoughtful compliment and future plan. Luenell's warm 'Good night, Borat' and his moved 'You say my name right' add unexpected tenderness.

jokes.text: Borat, deeply moved: 'You say my name right.'
jokes.setup: After offering to pay Luenell for sex, she says 'Good night, Borat' — pronouncing his name correctly
jokes.punchline: This simple act of correctly pronouncing his name moves Borat profoundly — implying that throughout his American journey, almost no one has gotten his name right
jokes.explanation: This is a quietly beautiful ending note. Four words carry a wealth of character pathos: throughout the reel, Borat has been misidentified, mistreated, nearly killed, and had his name mangled. Luenell — a sex worker he's just offered to pay — says his name correctly and it becomes the most meaningful interaction of his journey. The joke works as comedy (the bar set so low that correct pronunciation is profound) and as genuine emotional resonance. Character integration is exceptional — only Borat's particular loneliness and outsider status makes this land.

jokes.text: I needed a gift to give to Pamela so that she would grant me entry into her vagin.
jokes.setup: Borat frames a romantic gesture in transactional, crudely literal terms
jokes.punchline: The word 'vagin' (truncated/accented) makes the blunt sexuality simultaneously absurd and hilarious
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in-character for Borat: romantic intent expressed with the bluntness of a transaction and the linguistic stumble of 'vagin.' The truncation of the word is funnier than spelling it out. High character integration — only Borat says this.

jokes.text: Don't spend more than 3 dollars. We're low on money.
jokes.setup: They are about to enter a shop to find a gift for a woman Borat is pursuing across the country
jokes.punchline: The budget of $3 for a romantic gift reveals the duo's complete financial incompetence and sets up the destruction to come
jokes.explanation: A compact, efficient setup line that plants an absurd constraint. Gets funnier in retrospect once we see the $425 worth of damage. Functional comedy with good economy.

jokes.text: And this is just a little decorative derrick. And... do you think.. you know... when they...
jokes.setup: Shop owner is showing Borat around the antique shop; Borat is clearly about to touch something fragile
jokes.punchline: The trailing off and long pause (inferred from the gap to 51:26) suggests Borat has already begun breaking something — the owner's dawning horror is the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic slow-build cringe. The sentence trailing into silence while the shop owner watches Borat destroy something is a well-worn but effectively executed bit in the mockumentary format.

jokes.text: Don't worry, my friend... he can make glue...
jokes.setup: Azamat has apparently broken antiques worth hundreds of dollars
jokes.punchline: Borat's solution is that someone can 'make glue' — an absurdly inadequate response to the scale of the damage
jokes.explanation: The gap between the problem ($425 of damage) and Borat's proposed solution (glue) is perfectly calibrated absurdism. It's also believable as something Borat would genuinely think is helpful.

jokes.text: Ok, I have digital watch from the future. I will give you this. We are small than all of this. You broke 425$ worth of stuff.
jokes.setup: Shop owner demands payment for $425 of broken goods
jokes.punchline: Borat attempts to pay with 'a digital watch from the future' — a simultaneously absurd and pathetic barter
jokes.explanation: The 'digital watch from the future' is a genuinely original absurdist detail that elevates what could be a generic can't-pay bit. It reveals Borat's sincere belief that this is a fair trade, which is funnier than any self-aware joke could be.

jokes.text: This is the best hair in Kazakhstan. Feel the quality. — I don't want your damn hair. This hair from pubis. I can get you 2000 bags by next Friday.
jokes.setup: Borat is trying every possible means of payment for the broken antiques; cash isn't enough
jokes.punchline: Borat escalates from offering his own hair, to specifying it's pubic hair, to offering to supply 2,000 bags of it — a staggering escalation of wrongness
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional escalation comedy. Each step is funnier than the last: offering hair is strange, specifying pubic hair is shocking, offering 2,000 bags of it by next Friday suggests Borat has an ongoing pubic hair supply operation. The specificity ('2000 bags,' 'by next Friday') is what elevates this to genuine craft. The shop owner's disgusted reactions sell it perfectly. Comparable in structure to a great escalation joke.

jokes.text: You have ruined this documentary and almost bankrupt us! — So call the Ministry and get more money. — What?! If I did that they would kill us!
jokes.setup: Borat berates Azamat for breaking the antiques; Azamat suggests the logical solution of getting more funds
jokes.punchline: Borat reveals that contacting the Ministry would result in their deaths — a casual admission of authoritarian danger played for laughs
jokes.explanation: Solid dark comedy — the casual mention that contacting their government superiors would result in death is funny because Borat treats it as an obvious fact not worth dwelling on. Good character world-building.

jokes.text: How dare you make hand-party over Pamela! Why you don't care who I pleasure myself to? Because I love this woman!
jokes.setup: Borat has apparently caught Azamat masturbating to a Pamela Anderson photo/image
jokes.punchline: 'Hand-party' as a euphemism for masturbation is delightfully inventive; then the reveal that Azamat is also in love with Pamela Anderson creates a full comedic conflict
jokes.explanation: 'Hand-party' is one of the film's most quotable coinages — it perfectly captures Borat's linguistic creativity and his culture's euphemistic framing of sexuality. The subsequent reveal that Azamat loves Pamela too is a brilliant plot complication that also functions as a great joke. 'Because I love this woman!' delivered with full Azamat sincerity about a Baywatch star is excellent character comedy. High quotability score justified.

jokes.text: Lhal jsi o Kalifornii! (Czech/Slovak argument scene — Borat and Azamat fighting in their real language)
jokes.setup: Borat and Azamat's argument has been conducted in English for the audience's benefit; now they devolve into their actual language
jokes.punchline: The switch to what sounds like Czech/Slovak reveals the constructed nature of the film and also shows the fight has escalated beyond the performative — the unscripted reality bleeding through
jokes.explanation: A clever meta-joke for attentive viewers — the actors slip into their actual shared language (Czech, used by Cohen and Ken Davitian) mid-fight, puncturing the film's own fiction. Works better on rewatch when you know what's happening.

jokes.text: Eat my asshole!
jokes.setup: Borat and Azamat's argument has reached its peak
jokes.punchline: This particular insult — 'Eat my asshole!' — delivered with full conviction as a devastating parting shot, is both crude and oddly magnificent
jokes.explanation: It works primarily through conviction and economy — three words that end a scene. It's not a sophisticated joke but it's perfectly deployed as a punctuation mark. The humor comes from the gap between how seriously Borat means it and how absurd it sounds.

jokes.text: So.. bad news. Azamat leave.
jokes.setup: Borat needs to explain what happened after the fight
jokes.punchline: The profound understatement — 'bad news. Azamat leave' — to describe being abandoned in a foreign country with no money or passport
jokes.explanation: Classic Borat deadpan delivery — the magnitude of his situation reduced to the most minimal possible description. Good economy and character voice.

jokes.text: It's a hen.
jokes.setup: Azamat has left Borat various items; Borat lists them in a talking head
jokes.punchline: Among the items left behind is a live hen, presented with complete matter-of-factness
jokes.explanation: Three-word joke of perfect economy. The hen is never explained, never justified — it's just there. Borat's flat delivery ('It's a hen.') with zero surprise or confusion is what makes it land. The absurdity is entirely in the gap between what a normal person would leave a stranded partner and what Azamat has left.

jokes.text: my beautiful. Which I have cleaned since last night.
jokes.setup: Borat lists the few things Azamat left him — presumably his suit
jokes.punchline: The clarification that he has cleaned it 'since last night' implies it was in a state of serious uncleanliness prior, while also suggesting this is a point of pride
jokes.explanation: A quiet, understated character joke. The implication of what 'cleaned since last night' means given the events of the film is left entirely to the audience. Good economy and character voice.

jokes.text: Making without Azamat I think it will be better.
jokes.setup: Borat has just lost his producer, all his money, and his passport
jokes.punchline: He announces that making the documentary without Azamat will be an improvement — the delusional optimism landing as irony
jokes.explanation: Classic Borat delusional optimism. Works as character comedy but isn't the most original beat in the film.

jokes.text: making romance explosion on her stomach
jokes.setup: Borat describes his romantic dream of being with Pamela Anderson
jokes.punchline: 'Romance explosion on her stomach' is Borat's euphemism for ejaculation — the crude reality beneath the romantic framing delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: 'Romance explosion on her stomach' is genuinely exceptional coinage — the word 'romance' doing so much euphemistic work while 'explosion' supplies the crude specificity. It encapsulates everything about Borat's character: sincere romantic aspiration expressed through completely inappropriate directness. Highly quotable, entirely original, only Borat says this. Justified 8+ score.

jokes.text: So you like the bitches out there, in the fucking old Russia?
jokes.setup: Frat brothers are trying to bond with Borat and ask about women in Kazakhstan (which they call 'Russia')
jokes.punchline: The frat brother's casual use of 'bitches' and his conflation of Kazakhstan with Russia reveals his ignorance as genuine comedy — this is unscripted and therefore funnier
jokes.explanation: The humor here is observational/documentary — real American frat boys casually calling women 'bitches' and not knowing Kazakhstan isn't Russia. The comedy is in the revelation of genuine attitudes, which is the film's central satirical mechanism.

jokes.text: You fuck the shit out of me. And then you never call them again. — Why you don't call them, because they do not have a telephone, yes?
jokes.setup: Frat brother is explaining the hookup culture of 'fucking and not calling'
jokes.punchline: Borat interprets the reason for not calling as literally being that women in America don't have telephones — a perfect misunderstanding that also reveals something about Kazakhstan
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed misunderstanding joke. Borat's literal interpretation ('they do not have a telephone, yes?') perfectly subverts the punchline the frat brother was expecting, while simultaneously implying that women in Kazakhstan genuinely lack phones. The frat brother's confusion at having his bro-wisdom Borated is a perfect reaction beat. Near-8 quality.

jokes.text: Let me tell you game we play. We play game called When the snake eat the pig. You get a baby mouse, very small and you put a bit of cheese in hole of your hram until it go inside.
jokes.setup: Borat offers to share a Kazakh party game with the frat brothers
jokes.punchline: The game involves inserting a mouse into one's rectum ('hram') using cheese as bait — the deadpan procedural description of something deeply disturbing is the joke
jokes.explanation: Exceptional absurdist construction. The game has a name ('When the snake eat the pig'), coherent internal logic (cheese bait to lure mouse into rectum), and Borat's procedural delivery makes it funnier than any amount of winking could. The frat brother's response — 'That is too crazy for me' followed immediately by 'I'll do it' from another — is a perfect real-world reaction that the film couldn't have scripted better. High originality.

jokes.text: you get a baby mouse, very small and you… put a bit of cheese in hole of your hram until it go inside.
jokes.setup: Borat begins explaining the rules of 'When the snake eat the pig'
jokes.punchline: 'Hram' is apparently a body cavity; a baby mouse with cheese is inserted into it. The escalation from charming folk game to disturbing body horror is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: The reveal of what this game actually involves is a perfect escalation — the audience's imagination is worse than anything explicit. 'A bit of cheese in hole of your hram' is simultaneously absurd worldbuilding and body horror. The frat brother's immediate 'I'll do it' is the capper.

jokes.text: That is too crazy for me. — I'll do it. I'll go. Fuck, I'll do it.
jokes.setup: Borat has just described a deeply disturbing 'game' involving a mouse
jokes.punchline: One frat brother declines; another immediately volunteers with enthusiasm — a perfect documentary revelation of frat culture
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is entirely unscripted and purely observational. The juxtaposition of one person's refusal and another's immediate enthusiasm is funnier than any scripted response could be. The 'Fuck, I'll do it' captures genuine frat-bro peer pressure dynamics. Excellent because it's real.

jokes.text: Our country, the minorities actually have more power. Anyone that is minority has the upper hand. We have the Jews, anybody that's against mainstream.
jokes.setup: Borat has asked the frat brothers about slavery
jokes.punchline: The frat brother's deeply confused attempt to explain minority power — listing 'the Jews' as an example of a powerful minority — reveals real ignorance/attitudes unscripted for the camera
jokes.explanation: The comedy is deeply satirical — the frat brother's earnest explanation of minority power, culminating in 'we have the Jews' as his example of a powerful minority group, is both funny and disturbing in the film's characteristic way. The humor is in the gap between his confidence and his incoherence.

jokes.text: This my new wife. — You know her? — Pamela, I know of Pamela. — I will take her virgin for the first time. — I am going to put this shit on.
jokes.setup: Borat shows the frat brothers a photo of Pamela Anderson as his 'new wife'
jokes.punchline: The frat brothers immediately put on a Pamela Anderson sex tape — a perfect escalation of casual disrespect that also devastates Borat's romantic idealism
jokes.explanation: A multi-layered joke: Borat's sincere declaration ('I will take her virgin for the first time') is immediately undercut by the frat brothers putting on her sex tape. The gap between Borat's romantic fantasy and the crude reality delivered by the bros is perfect irony.

jokes.text: She is no virgin. — She is not.
jokes.setup: Borat has just declared he will 'take her virgin'; frat brothers have put on her sex tape
jokes.punchline: The simple, flat delivery of 'She is no virgin' as a devastating factual correction is perfectly understated
jokes.explanation: Economy does the heavy lifting here. The flat, factual correction of Borat's romantic delusion in four words is well-timed and lands as a punctuation mark.

jokes.text: Liar! Liar, liar, panties on fire!
jokes.setup: Borat has just been told Pamela is not a virgin, confirmed by visual evidence on the sex tape
jokes.punchline: Borat's response to the incontrovertible evidence is to invoke a children's rhyme — 'panties on fire' substituted for 'pants on fire' adds an accidental sexual dimension
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever: 'panties on fire' as a malapropism of 'pants on fire' works on multiple levels — it's a half-remembered American idiom, it's sexually resonant given the context (sex tape, virginity), and it perfectly captures Borat's child-like emotional reaction. Highly quotable. Good character integration — his sincere devastation makes the childish rhyme funnier.

jokes.text: What she doing? — She sucking some dick, man.
jokes.setup: Borat watches the sex tape with the frat brothers; asks what Pamela is doing
jokes.punchline: The completely casual, matter-of-fact answer from the frat brother is both funny and cringe-inducing
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy. The frat brother's total nonchalance vs. Borat's horror is the joke. Not particularly crafted but effective in context.

jokes.text: Come here. You're my man. You're my man. Come on, Borat. Stay with us, buddy. We'll remember you always. You in America now. You'll make it. You keep going. You're bigger than a woman. You're better than a woman.
jokes.setup: Borat is devastated by the revelation that Pamela is not a virgin; frat brothers comfort him
jokes.punchline: The frat brothers deliver heartfelt life advice to a foreign stranger about overcoming a woman — the advice is simultaneously sincere and deeply misogynistic, delivered with total straight-faced conviction
jokes.explanation: One of the film's best unscripted moments — these real frat brothers are genuinely trying to comfort Borat, and their advice ('You're bigger than a woman. You're better than a woman.') is both touching in intent and revealing in its casual sexism. The comedy comes from the sincerity of real people revealing their actual worldview.

jokes.text: Go. Run to freedom. Go! Go! I leave you alive.
jokes.setup: Borat appears to be releasing something into the wild — presumably the hen from earlier
jokes.punchline: 'I leave you alive' as the final mercy gift to an animal he's releasing is absurdly magnanimous and implies this is a significant concession on Borat's part
jokes.explanation: 'I leave you alive' is excellent economy — it implies Borat considered NOT leaving the hen alive and frames the act of release as a generous mercy. The absurdist dignity of the moment lands well.

jokes.text: I didn't evolve out of a monkey. I didn't use to be a..., I is what I is.
jokes.setup: Borat has arrived at a Pentecostal revival meeting; the preacher addresses the congregation
jokes.punchline: The preacher's anti-evolution speech ('I is what I is') is unscripted and reveals genuine beliefs — the comedy is in the gap between the confidence and the grammar
jokes.explanation: Unscripted observational comedy — the preacher's grammatically broken anti-evolution declaration ('I is what I is') is unintentionally ironic in a way that couldn't be scripted. The humor is in the real, not the constructed.

jokes.text: I have no friends, I am alone in this country. Nobody like me. My only friend Azamat he take my money and my bear and he leave me alone.
jokes.setup: Borat has gone to the altar of a Pentecostal revival to confess his troubles
jokes.punchline: The cascade of misfortunes — including that his friend took 'my money AND my bear' — delivered with sincere grief in front of a congregation expecting religious testimony
jokes.explanation: The bear is the detail that makes this — not just 'my money' but 'my money AND my bear.' The congregation receiving this as a sincere spiritual testimony creates a beautiful cringe comedy tension. Borat's grief is real (within the fiction) and the congregation's earnest response is perfectly absurd.

jokes.text: Do Jesus love my retard brother, Bilok? — He loves your brother Bilok.
jokes.setup: Borat is testing the limits of Jesus's love by listing increasingly specific cases
jokes.punchline: The addition of 'my retard brother Bilok' as a test case — delivered with complete sincerity — and the preacher's earnest confirmation pushes the bit into genuine dark comedy
jokes.explanation: Part of a well-constructed escalating sequence. The name 'Bilok' adds absurdist specificity. The preacher's straight-faced responses to increasingly specific questions about who Jesus loves creates a beautiful running gag structure within the scene.

jokes.text: Do Jesus love my neighbour, Nusultan Tuliakbai? — Yes, he loves everybody. — Nobody love my neighbour Nusultan Taliakbai.
jokes.setup: The preacher has affirmed that Jesus loves everyone including Borat's specific neighbors
jokes.punchline: Borat's flat correction — 'Nobody love my neighbour Nusultan Taliakbai' — implies this neighbor is so universally disliked that even Jesus's love would be an anomaly
jokes.explanation: One of the film's funniest lines. The structure is perfect: the preacher sets up with 'he loves everybody,' and Borat's flat correction ('Nobody love my neighbour Nusultan Taliakbai') subverts it by implying this neighbor is SO bad that even divine universal love would be an exception. The name itself is funny, the callback to a recurring character adds layers, and the deadpan delivery is flawless. The fact that this plays in front of an evangelical congregation makes it funnier. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Let that tongue go! Here comes! Let that tongue go!
jokes.setup: The congregation is trying to bring Borat into a speaking-in-tongues spiritual experience
jokes.punchline: The preacher's urging ('Let that tongue go!') followed by what we can infer is Borat speaking in tongues in Kazakh — the religious ceremony's mechanics applied to a foreign language create absurdist comedy
jokes.explanation: The speaking-in-tongues scene works as extended cringe comedy — the congregation's genuine religious fervor meets Borat's probable performance of Kazakh as glossolalia. The juxtaposition is rich but the transcript doesn't give us Borat's actual tongue contribution, limiting the score.

jokes.text: I will forgive Pamela. And I will go to California. I will go to Malibu with me and my friend, mister Jesus. And together, we will take her.
jokes.setup: Borat has just had a religious experience at the Pentecostal revival
jokes.punchline: His spiritual renewal is immediately redirected toward his original sexual goal — 'we will take her' — with Jesus now conscripted as an accomplice
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent joke construction. The religious scene has built to Borat's spiritual renewal — and the punchline is that nothing has changed except Jesus is now his wingman. 'My friend, mister Jesus' is perfect Borat register, and 'we will take her' redirects the divine toward the carnal in a way that's both funny and character-defining. Strong structure, high character integration.

jokes.text: I will forgive Pamela. And I will go to California. I will go to Malibu with me and my friend, mister Jesus. And together, we will take her.
jokes.setup: The Pentecostal revival has worked on Borat; he announces his renewed purpose
jokes.punchline: 'And together, we will take her' — Jesus is now Borat's wingman in the pursuit of Pamela Anderson; the sacred and profane are fused with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The religious revival being immediately redirected toward the goal of sleeping with a celebrity is both satirically sharp and perfectly in character. 'Mr. Jesus' as a formal title, and Jesus as an active co-conspirator in the seduction, is inspired absurdism. The congregation presumably heard this announcement.

jokes.text: Azamat? You traitor! Look, I can explain! You attack me. My mustache still tastes of your ass!
jokes.setup: Borat has found Azamat again at a Hollywood costume party; they haven't spoken since the fight
jokes.punchline: 'My mustache still tastes of your ass!' — a visceral, specific grievance delivered as an opening statement that immediately tells us everything about how their previous fight ended
jokes.explanation: One of the film's best lines. 'My mustache still tastes of your ass' is a perfect callback that fills in the gap of what happened during/after their fight — something so specific and visceral that it functions as both exposition and joke simultaneously. The specificity of the mustache detail is what elevates this above generic crude humor. Highly quotable, completely original, earned through the narrative context.

jokes.text: Well, that's another fine mess you've gotten me into.
jokes.setup: Azamat and Borat have just been in a scuffle at the costume party
jokes.punchline: Azamat quotes the classic Laurel and Hardy catchphrase — a moment of meta-comedy where the film's own absurdist double-act acknowledges its slapstick heritage
jokes.explanation: Clever meta-reference — Azamat/Ken Davitian is physically not unlike Oliver Hardy, and the quote acknowledges the Borat-Azamat dynamic as a classic comic duo. Works on multiple levels for film-literate audiences.

jokes.text: I have not come to Hollywood to fight a man dressed as Hitler.
jokes.setup: Borat and Azamat have just fought at what turns out to be a costume party; Borat is explaining his purpose
jokes.punchline: The completely reasonable statement that he didn't come to Hollywood to fight a man dressed as Hitler — implying that IS what just happened — is absurdist gold
jokes.explanation: One of the film's best lines. The joke works on three levels: (1) the absurdist image of fighting someone dressed as Hitler at a Hollywood party, (2) Borat's reasonable-sounding protest that implies he has DONE exactly that, (3) the economy — the entire scene is explained in one sentence. The addition of 'dressed as Hitler' rather than any other costume is both the funniest specific choice and a perfect Borat-world detail. Near-exceptional.

jokes.text: What? A woman has written a book? Dr. Yamak would never believe this.
jokes.setup: Azamat shows Borat that Pamela Anderson is doing a book signing
jokes.punchline: Borat's genuine astonishment that a woman has authored a book — delivered as news worthy of sharing with 'Dr. Yamak' — is both funny as character comedy and pointed as satire
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — the specificity of 'Dr. Yamak would never believe this' adds a world-building detail (there is a Dr. Yamak back home who shares these views) that makes it funnier than a generic sexist comment. Borat's sincere amazement is what sells it.

jokes.text: My name Borat Sagdiyev, I son of Sagdiyev, and Boltok the rapist, my former husband of Oksana Sagdiyev who was daughter of Tarekbai and Boltok the rapist.
jokes.setup: Borat introduces himself to Pamela Anderson at her book signing in the traditional Kazakh way
jokes.punchline: 'Boltok the rapist' appears twice in the family tree — both as former husband and presumably as grandfather figure — presented as an ordinary family name/title
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'Boltok the rapist' in both positions of the family tree — delivered with the seriousness of a formal introduction — is excellent dark comedy. The formal register of the genealogical recitation makes the content funnier. It's a perfect Borat moment: sincere, specific, and deeply wrong.

jokes.text: Pamela, will you marry me? — No thanks, sorry.
jokes.setup: Borat has just presented a marriage contract and introduced himself with full Kazakh formality
jokes.punchline: Pamela Anderson's completely casual, almost bored refusal — 'No thanks, sorry' — deflates the entire romantic quest built over the film
jokes.explanation: The punchline earns its score through economy and structural perfection. The entire film has been building to this proposal; Borat's formal Kazakh introduction, the wedding sack, the film's journey across America — all collapsed by 'No thanks, sorry.' The casualness of Pamela's refusal (she barely looks up) is the joke. Perfect economy: four words end the quest.

jokes.text: Pamela... Don't worry... I never stood... my wife. Pamela, I will give you your own plow.
jokes.setup: Borat is trying to convince Pamela Anderson to marry him despite her refusal; he is reassuring her
jokes.punchline: 'I will give you your own plow' as a romantic incentive — an agricultural concession that reveals the gap between Borat's world and the world he's in
jokes.explanation: 'Your own plow' as a romantic offering to a Malibu celebrity is a perfect culture-clash joke. The word 'own' suggests this is a significant concession in Kazakh marital terms. High character integration — only Borat's world produces this incentive.

jokes.text: Pamela, I am not attracted to you any more! — NOT!
jokes.setup: Borat has been restrained by security during his attempt to bag Pamela in the wedding sack
jokes.punchline: He delivers what sounds like a dignified parting shot — 'I am not attracted to you any more!' — then immediately negates it with 'NOT!' in the fashion of a 1990s schoolyard joke
jokes.explanation: The 'NOT!' joke is a deliberately dated construction — using the Wayne's World/early-90s format as Borat's most sophisticated rhetorical maneuver is both funny and character-perfect. It's a joke about how Borat's understanding of American culture is filtered through dated pop culture he's absorbed.

jokes.text: The great times. The good times. And the shit times. Mainly there were shit times.
jokes.setup: Borat reflects on his journey across America
jokes.punchline: The expected tripartite structure ('great... good... shit') is immediately undercut by the flat qualification: 'Mainly there were shit times'
jokes.explanation: Elegant joke construction — the tripartite setup (great/good/shit) with the immediate flat deflation ('mainly there were shit times') is a great comedic rhythm. The honesty of the self-assessment is funnier than any exaggeration would be. High economy.

jokes.text: I have learned that if you chase a dream, especially one with plastic chests, you can miss the real beauty in front of your eyes.
jokes.setup: Borat delivers the film's supposed moral lesson from his journey
jokes.punchline: 'Especially one with plastic chests' inserted into the inspirational formula collapses the sentimental register and reveals Borat's journey was always primarily about Pamela Anderson's augmented appearance
jokes.explanation: One of the film's best-constructed lines. It uses the template of a genuine inspirational observation and subverts it perfectly with 'especially one with plastic chests' — which simultaneously (1) deflates the sentimentality, (2) reveals Borat's sincere fixation, and (3) works as a comedic callback to the entire Pamela plot. The structure (setup the formula, corrupt it in the middle, pay off at end) is textbook good joke construction.

jokes.text: We no longer here running of the jew, it's cruel. We christians now.
jokes.setup: Borat provides an update on his hometown's improvements since his return
jokes.punchline: The 'improvement' that they've stopped the 'running of the jew' because it's cruel — not because it's antisemitic — and the replacement of this practice with Christianity is a perfect dark satire of performative moral progress
jokes.explanation: Exceptional dark satirical construction. The joke works on multiple layers: (1) the callback to the 'Running of the Jew' established earlier in the film, (2) the reason for stopping being 'it's cruel' rather than 'it's antisemitic' — a parody of performative moral improvement without actual moral understanding, (3) replacing it with Christianity as an 'upgrade' satirizes American missionary influence. This is the film's satirical mechanism at its sharpest. Justified 8+ score.

jokes.text: Toktan improve too. Hey, Toktan. Hi 5!
jokes.setup: Borat narrates improvements in his village; Toktan is apparently a villager with some disability or distinctive characteristic
jokes.punchline: The 'Hi 5!' suggests Toktan has learned the American greeting — an absurd image of American cultural imperialism reduced to a high-five
jokes.explanation: A quick visual/character joke that works as part of the 'improvements' montage. The specificity of the high-five as the emblem of American cultural learning is sharp, though the joke is underdeveloped in transcript form.

jokes.text: There Nusultan Tudialkbai. He's still asshole.
jokes.setup: Borat is narrating improvements in his village; Nusultan has been a recurring figure of contempt
jokes.punchline: 'He's still asshole' — the flat, unapologetic assessment delivered as an objective fact among the other village updates
jokes.explanation: The running gag on Nusultan pays off perfectly here. The structure — village has improved, Toktan has improved, 'he's still asshole' — is a perfect comedic rhythm (setup improvements, one flat exception). The economy is exceptional: three words to deliver a callback, a character judgment, and a punchline simultaneously. The article-less 'He's still asshole' rather than 'an asshole' is the linguistic detail that makes it funnier.

jokes.text: I get iPod, he only get iPod Mini. Everybody know is for girls.
jokes.setup: Borat is describing his status advantage over his hated neighbor Nusultan
jokes.punchline: The ultimate marker of Borat's triumph over his nemesis is having a full-sized iPod vs. the iPod Mini — 'everybody know is for girls' delivered with complete conviction
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever satirical joke — Borat's triumph over his nemesis is measured in the terms of American consumer culture (iPod vs. iPod Mini), and his confident assertion that the Mini 'is for girls' satirizes both gender-coded consumer products and the way American materialism has been absorbed into Kazakh village life. The specificity of the iPod Mini as the marker of lesser status is perfect. Well-constructed final joke.

jokes.text: And this my beautiful wife. — Luenell (the sex worker from earlier in the film appears as Borat's wife)
jokes.setup: Borat says he found 'real beauty in front of his eyes' rather than chasing Pamela Anderson
jokes.punchline: His 'beautiful wife' is revealed to be the sex worker character from earlier in the film — a perfect callback that pays off the film's moral while simultaneously undercutting it
jokes.explanation: The film's final joke is its best structural construction. The 'moral' (don't chase a dream, find real beauty in front of you) is paid off by revealing the 'real beauty' is a sex worker from earlier in the film. It simultaneously (1) validates the moral on its own absurd terms (he found love!), (2) completely undercuts any sentimental reading, (3) rewards attentive viewers with a callback, and (4) is a perfect Borat-logic conclusion. Near the top of the episode's scoring.
